newsitem.title: GABON: Cocoa ministers to agree three-year output plans.
newsitem.headline: Cocoa ministers to agree three-year output plans.

text.p: Cocoa ministers reviewing the 1993 International Cocoa Agreement will agree output plans for the next three years this week at a meeting in Gabon but some producers want forecasts affecting them reviewed.

"We have already agreed output cuts with the ICCO (International Cocoa Organisation) but some figures need minor reviews," Cocoa Producers Alliance (CPA) Secretary-General Silas Kanga told Reuters ahead of this week's talks.
Members facing output cuts under an ICCO agreement to shave 90,000 tonnes off total world output over the next three years want forecasts used for their countries' yields revised.

In September, the ICCO, which groups producers and consumers, agreed to cut production by 15,000 tonnes in 1996/97, 30,000 tonnes in 1997/98 and 45,000 tonnes in 1998/99 to help balance world supply and demand.
Malaysian CPA delelgates at a meeting of experts in Gabon's capital Libreville last week said the ICCO forecast used for Malasian output over the period was too low.

"The ICCO says we will produce 117,000 tonnes next year, but our unprofitable areas are now out of production and rehabilitation will raise output," primary industries ministry official Ahma Buang told Reuters.
CPA member forecasts presented at the talks showed Malaysia's output rising to 130,000 tonnes in 1996/97 from 122,000 tonnes and then by 10,000 tonnes a year to 150,000 tonnes in 1998/99.
London trader ED & F Man put Malaysia's 1995/96 yield at 105,000 tonnes due to a reduction in the size of cocoa areas.
Delegates said other countries had also requested reviews.
"The (ICCO) econometric model cannot predict changing rain patterns so forecasts are open to discussion," said one.

CPA member forecasts show Ivory Coast's production rising by 50,000 tonnes from 900,000 tonnes in 1996/97. Ghana's yield is shown rising from 350,000 tonnes in 1996/97 to 380,000 tonnes in 1997/98 and then 400,000 tonnes in 1998/99.
Yields in Brazil and Ecuador are seen as stable over the period, at 215,000 and 104,000 tonnes respectively.
Over the same period CPA member forecasts show output overall falling to 2,574,000 tonnes in 1996/97 from 2,757,000 in 1995/96, and then rising to 2,667,000 in 1997/98 and 2,767,000 in 1998/98.
Cocoa producer ministers will announce their decisions on Wednesday after reviewing the governing 1993 pact on Monday and Tuesday.
Ministers will also decide producers' tactics over European Union proposals to boost non-cocoa fat usage.
"Our position on cocoa fats is already known," Kanga said.

"World stocks are high enough and there will be enough cocoa around. We don't see the justification," said Kanga, pointing to ICCO estimates of world stocks of 1,198,000 tonnes, equal to about five months of expected 1996/97 grindings.
Kanga said demand for cocoa beans would drop by 200,000 tonnes if the European Union approved use of non-cocoa fat from next year, but one delgate disagreed with the figure.

"It wouldn't be that much. New products and markets might even increase demand," said a Malaysian official. "The real problem is checking how much and what type of non-vegetable substitute is being used."
Kanga said ministers would also discuss reports of contamination of cocoa beans by jute bag odours.
